sections.html: Hemidoras stenopeltis (Kner, 1855), the Mouse Catfish. Size: 12.5 cm SL. Type locality: Rio Negro, Amazon system, Brazil. Synonym: Doras stenopeltis.
Dense vegetation gives this fish a much-needed sense of confidence in its surroundings. Caves or dark refuges appear less important.

Until acclimatized, the fish appears quite selective and likes small foods. Crushed flake or sinking flake-based tablets are best for smaller individuals, although brine shrimp is taken by fish around 5 cm. Larger, more settled fish are easier to feed and become very active during feeding.

Not aggressive and, as with all doradids, sociable with its own species. Smaller fish appear to have an innate fear of larger fish and become very shy in their presence.

Suggested tankmates: shoaling tetras and Brochis are ideal. Dwarf cichlids and smaller labyrinth fish (gouramis etc.) are also suitably gentle. Larger, acclimatized fish do well in a medium to large community tank. At any size, best kept in shoals to ensure greater boldness and health.
Adult males have what seems to be an enlarged dorsal spine. This is however a filament (as can be seen, for instance, in Synodontis decora). Females lack this feature.

The black top mouse catfish is very similar to another mouse catfish, Nemadoras leporhinus, the main visual difference being the latter's clear dorsal fin with a black marking at its base. N. leporhinus also has longer leading fin rays. Key characters: deep plates, pointed humeral process (rounded in Leptodoras), short pointed snout, plates along the back (also along the ventral midline before the anal fin) and the tip of the dorsal fin dipped in black.
